conversation.question: Can you tell me about a time you worked on a team project and what your specific role was?
conversation.answer: In my third-year software engineering course, I was part of a team of four building a REST API for a library management system. I took on the role of backend lead, designing the database schema and implementing the core CRUD endpoints using Python and Flask. I also set up our CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions so we could catch bugs early.

conversation.question: What was the most challenging technical decision you had to make during that project?
conversation.answer: The hardest decision was choosing between a relational database and a document store. We initially leaned toward MongoDB because it seemed simpler, but after analyzing our data relationships I convinced the team to use PostgreSQL. This ended up being the right call because we had complex joins for the book-borrower-reservation relationships, and our query performance was about 3x faster than our initial MongoDB prototype.

conversation.question: Describe a situation where you had to learn a new technology quickly to complete a task.
conversation.answer: During a hackathon last semester, our team decided to build a real-time chat application using WebSockets. I had never used WebSockets before, so I spent the first two hours reading the Socket.IO documentation and following a tutorial. By the end of the 24-hour hackathon, I had implemented the real-time messaging feature and we won second place.

conversation.question: How did you validate that your WebSocket implementation was working correctly under load?
conversation.answer: Honestly, we didn't do formal load testing during the hackathon due to time constraints. But I did write some basic integration tests that simulated multiple concurrent connections. I used Python's asyncio to create 20 simultaneous clients sending messages and verified that all messages were delivered in order. After the hackathon, I went back and added proper load testing with Locust, which showed our implementation could handle about 500 concurrent users on a single instance.

conversation.question: Tell me about a time you received critical feedback and how you responded to it.
conversation.answer: In my internship at TechStart Inc., my supervisor reviewed my first pull request and pointed out that my code lacked proper error handling and had no unit tests. At first I felt defensive, but I scheduled a one-on-one to understand their expectations better. I then rewrote the module with comprehensive error handling and added pytest tests with 90% coverage. My supervisor later used my refactored code as an example of good practices for other interns.

conversation.question: What specific testing practices did you adopt after that experience?
conversation.answer: I started writing tests before implementation using TDD for critical paths. I also adopted the AAA pattern — Arrange, Act, Assert — which made my tests much more readable. In my subsequent projects, I maintained at least 80% code coverage and set up pre-commit hooks to run the test suite before every push. This practice caught several regressions before they made it to the main branch.
